title: Design a Lazy Segment Tree
statement_md:
Updating one element of an array and reading one element back are both easy. The
awkward case is when *both* sides are ranges: add `delta` to every element between
`lo` and `hi`, then ask for the sum or the minimum of some other range. Doing
either one by touching every element costs `O(n)`, and the two requirements pull
against each other — a prefix-sum array answers sums instantly but has to be
rebuilt after any update.

A **segment tree** stores an aggregate for every node of a recursive halving of
the array, so any range decomposes into `O(log n)` nodes. That alone is not enough
here: a range update would still have to reach every leaf it covers. The fix is
**lazy propagation** — when an update covers a node's whole range, record the
pending change on that node and stop. The tag is pushed down to the children only
when a later call actually needs to look inside. Both operations then stay
`O(log n)`.

Implement the `LazySegmentTree` class:

- `LazySegmentTree(nums)` builds the structure over a copy of `nums`.
- `range_add(lo, hi, delta)` adds `delta` to every element with index in
  `[lo, hi]`, inclusive at both ends. It returns nothing.
- `range_sum(lo, hi)` returns the sum of the elements in `[lo, hi]`.
- `range_min(lo, hi)` returns the smallest element in `[lo, hi]`.
- `to_list()` returns the current array, with every pending update applied.

Both `range_min` and `range_sum` are asked for on purpose. A sum can be undone —
knowing the sum of `[0, hi]` and of `[0, lo - 1]` gives you the sum of `[lo, hi]`
— which is what lets prefix-based structures like a Fenwick tree answer sums
without ever storing a range. A minimum cannot: no amount of arithmetic recovers
`min(a[3..7])` from `min(a[0..7])` and `min(a[0..2])`. Keeping both in the API is
what forces a structure that stores aggregates *per range* rather than per prefix.

Unlike the other from-scratch structures in this catalog, nothing here reports the
internal shape, and that is deliberate: whether a pending tag has already been
pushed down to a child is invisible from the outside and changes no answer, so
there is no honest way to pin it. The specification is the results, and the
constraints are what make an `O(n)`-per-operation array good enough to be correct
but not good enough to be interesting.
constraints: At most $10^4$ calls total will be made to `range_add`, `range_sum`, `range_min`, and `to_list`.

solutions.title: Approach 1: Segment Tree With Lazy Propagation
solutions.intuition_md:
Build the recursive halving of the array and store, at every node, the sum and the
minimum of the range it covers. A query for `[ql, qr]` walks down from the root
with one of three outcomes at each node: the node's range is disjoint from the
query and contributes nothing, or it is entirely inside the query and contributes
its stored aggregate whole, or it straddles the edge and has to be split. Only the
straddling case recurses, and a range can straddle at most two nodes per level, so
a query touches `O(log n)` nodes.

An update has exactly the same three cases — and that symmetry is the idea. When a
node's range is entirely inside the update, its own sum and minimum can be fixed
in `O(1)`: add `delta * length` to the sum, `delta` to the minimum. The only
reason to keep descending would be to fix the children, and nobody is looking at
them yet.

So don't. Leave a **pending tag** on the node saying "everyone below me still owes
`delta`", and pay it only when a later call has to descend through this node. That
is lazy propagation, and it is what makes a range update cost the same `O(log n)`
as a range query instead of `O(range length)`.

The invariant that keeps this straight is worth stating exactly, because every bug
in a lazy segment tree is a violation of it: **a node's own stored aggregates are
always correct; its tag is what its children have not been told yet.**
solutions.algorithm_md:
Three flat arrays of size `4n` — `sums`, `mins`, `lazy` — with node `1` as the
root and node `i`'s children at `2i` and `2i + 1`. `4n` is the standard safe size:
the recursion is not a perfect binary tree unless `n` is a power of two, and `4n`
covers the worst case without any index arithmetic.

Two helpers carry the invariant:

- `_apply(node, lo, hi, delta)` settles a whole range at one node:
  `sums[node] += delta * (hi - lo + 1)`, `mins[node] += delta`, and
  `lazy[node] += delta`. The multiplication by the range length is why the node
  has to know its own bounds; the tags accumulate by addition because two pending
  adds compose into one.
- `_push(node, lo, mid, hi)` hands a non-zero tag to both children with `_apply`
  and clears it. Every method calls this immediately before recursing, which is
  what makes it safe for the rest of the code to read a child's aggregates
  directly.

`_add`, `_sum` and `_min` are then the same three-way walk: return the identity
(`0`, `None`) if disjoint, return the stored aggregate if fully covered, otherwise
push and recurse. `_add` finishes by recomputing the node from its children, since
the update changed them.

`to_list` does not recurse per element — that would be `O(n log n)`. It walks the
tree once with an explicit stack, carrying the sum of the tags seen on the way
down, and reads each leaf as `mins[leaf] + carried`. Note it accumulates the tag
*before* descending but not at the leaf itself: by the invariant, a leaf's own
value is already correct.
solutions.time_complexity: O(n)\text{ to build, } O(\log n)\text{ per range operation}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: A range straddles the boundary of at most two nodes per level, so both the update and the query visit O(log n) nodes; the lazy tag is what keeps an update from having to reach the leaves it covers. to_list is a single O(n) walk.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Three arrays of 4n entries, plus O(log n) recursion depth. The 4n is the standard safe bound for the implicit layout when n is not a power of two.

solutions.title: Approach 2: Square-Root Decomposition
solutions.intuition_md:
A segment tree splits the array `log n` times. Splitting it *once*, into blocks of
about `sqrt(n)` elements, already does most of the work — and it is much less code.

Keep the raw array, plus per block a sum, a minimum, and a pending add. Any range
covers at most two partial blocks at its ends and some number of whole blocks in
between. The partial ends are handled by looping over their elements directly; the
whole blocks in the middle are handled by their stored aggregates, exactly as a
segment tree handles a fully-covered node. There are at most `sqrt(n)` blocks and
at most `2*sqrt(n)` loose elements, so every operation is `O(sqrt(n))`.

This is worth knowing not as a fallback but because of what the measurements say.
`O(sqrt(n))` is asymptotically worse than `O(log n)`, and yet the loops over the
partial ends here are `sum()` and `min()` over a list slice — C-level operations
with almost no per-element cost — while the segment tree pays a Python function
call at every node it visits. At this problem's limits that trade favours the
blocks: measured on the shipped test data, this approach runs in roughly half the
time of Approach 1. The crossover is real but sits far past where this problem
stops, around `n` in the low hundreds of thousands.

The honest summary is that Approach 1 is the right structure and Approach 2 is the
faster program here, and knowing which of those two facts a given situation cares
about is most of the skill.
solutions.algorithm_md:
Block size `b` is the smallest integer with `b * b >= n`. Alongside `data`, three
per-block lists: `block_sum` and `block_min` over the **raw** values in `data`, and
`block_add`, the pending add. Keeping the aggregates raw and adding `block_add`
back at read time is what keeps updates `O(1)` per whole block; the alternative —
folding the pending add into the stored aggregate — has to be undone carefully
whenever an element is touched individually, and is where this approach usually
goes wrong.

- `range_add` writes the two partial ends straight into `data` and calls
  `_rebuild` on those two blocks, then bumps `block_add` for each whole block in
  between. When `lo` and `hi` land in the same block there is no middle, so it
  degenerates to a plain loop.
- `range_sum` adds `sum(slice)` plus `block_add * (number of elements taken)` for
  each partial end, and `block_sum[j] + block_add[j] * size` for each whole block.
  The last block can be short, hence the `min((j + 1) * b, n)` when computing its
  size.
- `range_min` is the same walk with `min` — and here the pending add contributes
  just once, not once per element, which is the small asymmetry between a sum and
  a minimum showing up in code.
- `to_list` reads each element as `data[i] + block_add[i // b]`.

`_rebuild(j)` recomputes one block's raw sum and minimum from its slice, and is
the only `O(sqrt(n))` write in the structure.
solutions.time_complexity: O(n)\text{ to build, } O(\sqrt{n})\text{ per range operation}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: At most two partial blocks of under sqrt(n) elements each, plus at most sqrt(n) whole blocks settled in constant time apiece. That is asymptotically worse than Approach 1, but the partial ends are C-level sum and min over a list slice while the segment tree pays a Python call per node, so on this problem's data it measures about twice as fast; the crossover sits around n in the low hundreds of thousands.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: The array itself plus three lists of about sqrt(n) entries, and no recursion at all.
